transcript: In 2019, the BBC published a trashy story about  one of Mainland China's largest landfills. The Jiangcungou (江村沟垃圾填埋场) in the  city of Xi'an, the story goes,   had run out of capacity some  25 years ahead of schedule. That year, China had about 400 incineration  and waste-to-energy plants. About 50% of the   country's municipal solid waste  was processed by incineration. Six years later, the Chinese situation is  a lot more interesting. In 2025, China has   over 1,137 incineration plants and over 80% of  Chinese municipal solid waste is incinerated. The country has about 1.2 million tons of daily  incineration capacity, but just 700,000 tons of   daily waste collection capacity. Thus, mothballed  capacity plus counties digging up old landfills. Human history has never seen a more furious span  of incinerator building. How did China build   700 incinerator plants in six years? In today's  video, a look at China's 2020s incinerator boom. ## Burn It We burn our municipal solid  waste for several reasons. A major one is that we want to reduce the volume  of the waste. Incineration leaves behind a pile of   ashes that is about 25-30% of its former size  - saving a significant bit of landfill space. For Asia's megacities, which have limited  space, this is huge. A perfect example is   what’s happening in Seoul. At the start  of 2026, local governments were banned   from putting solid waste directly into landfills  without incineration, because of dwindling space. Burning the waste also helps keep the landfill  stable and somewhat clean. It removes smells   that can make landfills unpleasant places  to be around. And it burns down organic   trash that can lead to potentially explosive  waste gas or shifting land, causing disasters. The most infamous being the  December 2015 incident in Shenzhen,   when landfilled construction waste slid down  as an avalanche - killing at least 73 people. One can argue certain environmental  benefits. Landfills generate amounts   of methane and carbon dioxide as  things decay. So while burning   the trash does contribute some amount of  greenhouse gases, it can prevent some too. And finally, we can use this waste as a  renewable energy source: Waste-to-energy. ## Waste-to-Energy Waste-to-energy systems work like  any other thermal power station.   It burns waste to make steam that turns a turbine. There are several categories. The most common  is the "moving grate". Here, the waste fuel is   put onto a downwards-sloping moving grate  - kind of like an escalator - that slowly   transports and mixes the material as it passes  through the processing and incineration steps. First there is a drying step. The waste material  is dried with hot air passing above and fire   coming up from below through the grate. We want to  remove water content, as that can dampen heating. There may or may not be a shredding  step - one of the strengths of the   moving grate is that it doesn't  necessarily need pre-shredding. Then the waste hits the combustion chamber  where it sits for at least 2 seconds at   temperatures of 850 to 1,100 degrees Celsius.  If the items are potentially hazardous - like   plastics that contain chlorine - then  we opt for the higher temperatures. The remaining ash drops down through  a chute at the end. Energy leaves the   furnace as flue gas and boils water  inside a boiler. Steam then goes to   a turbine before returning to liquid form.  The flue gas goes on for post-processing. I for some reason was reminded of the  Toy Story 3 incinerator so I went and   checked. But unfortunately that one seems to be  a simple open pit - apparently for story reasons. A real moving grate, I suppose, would  not have been as dramatic but now I am   concerned for Andy's neighborhood. This  plant is probably very heavily polluting. The Moving Grate is the most common  waste-to-energy plant, but there are others. The Circulating Fluidized Bed is an  alternative that feeds waste into a   chamber of hot fluidized sand.  It tends to be more efficient. Speaking of, waste-to-energy plants are  generally less efficient than today's   advanced fossil fuel-fired thermal plants  at about 30% or lower compared to 40-ish%. This is because the steam does not get  as hot - about 400 degrees compared to   600 degrees Celsius. That is because waste-derived   flue gases are quite corrosive due to  the presence of chlorine in plastics. The Chinese government turned to  incineration and waste-to-energy not   to make more power but for a practical  reason. During the economic boom days,   the country was generating more trash  than it can bury into landfills. ## Chinese Trash Boom In 1981, China collected about 26  million tons of municipal solid waste. To put that into context, the United States that  year generated six times as much municipal solid   waste despite at that time having only a  quarter as many people. Those two numbers   are not exactly one-to-one - collected is not  the same as generated - but you get the point. Before the opening up, people didn’t make  that much waste. They were poor. And the   solid waste that those people produced was  mostly organic - kitchen food waste, what not.   This is characteristic of developing  countries and non-urban populations. But China’s rapid development  and urbanization changed both   the amount of waste and its  composition. The amount grew   at about 8-10% annually. No country has  ever experienced such rapid waste growth. In 2004, Mainland China surpassed the  United States as the world's largest   generator of municipal solid waste.  By 2014, the amount of solid waste   reached 178 million tons - nearly seven  times higher than what it was in 1981. The waste composition also changed. There is still  a lot of organic material, but also more plastic,   paper and metal. Containers, bottles, whatever.  Some recycling is done by informal workers,   but low material prices makes  that relatively unprofitable. Projections made by the World Bank  in 2018 predicted that by 2030,   China will be generating twice as much as trash  as the US. Where are they going to put all that? ## Landfill? More Like LandFAIL Traditionally, the dumping ground for  all this trash has been the landfill. Early ones used cement liners, but  trash stored there tended to leak   toxic chemicals into the groundwater.  More modern landfills equipped with   high-density polyethylene liners  did not emerge until the 1990s. But city governments struggled to bring enough  official landfills online. You don't just cordon   off an area and start dumping trash. Done  right, a landfill is a multi-year project. You must survey environmental and groundwater  risks. Then build access roads and install liners   to prevent leachate flow, waste gas amelioration  infrastructure, and monitoring equipment. Since the official landfills can't  keep up, people and companies made   illegal landfills and open-air  dumps. Before you know it,   200 Chinese cities are surrounded by garbage  - causing safety hazards to residents. This is a situation other major  land-scarce countries have faced   before. Mega-cities like Tokyo,  Seoul and Singapore have turned   to incinerators as a technological  solution. Thusly so did China. ## The Incinerator Lights Up Mainland China's first modern incinerator  was built in Shenzhen in 1985. This incinerator had capacity  of about 500 tons per day,   and was provided by the Japanese  company Mitsubishi Heavy Industries. Mitsubishi Heavy in turn licensed  their technology from the German   company MARTIN in the 1970s when Japan  adopted incinerators. The two companies   often work together, combining Japanese  manufacturing with German engineering. But in the 2000s, incineration  and waste-to-energy plants were   not widely adopted. In 2002, just 3.7% of  China's collected waste was incinerated.   7% was composted, leaving all the rest  - well over 85% - to be landfilled. There were attenuating factors. Chinese  urban households generate a fair amount   of organic trash, as I mentioned. Organics  are 60-80% water, which causes problems for   incineration as water absorbs thermal  energy - dampening its heating value. There were also economic issues. A waste-to-energy  plant has far higher capital costs at about   $66,000 to $120,000 per ton of daily capacity  - with some going as high as $365,000. That high number is more of a developed  country estimate. These figures come out   of the World Bank's Decision Maker’s Guides  for Solid Waste Management Technologies, 2018. A landfill by comparison costs about $5,000 to   $20,000 per daily ton of capacity  over its lifetime. So all in all,   it is 5-10 times cheaper to make a landfill.  Even less if that landfill is an illegal one. ## Besieged by Waste A fierce debate raged early on - with  many saying that not addressing the   core issue of waste generation  is only treating the symptoms. Without proper recycling, collection  or fees to incentivize reduction,   incineration just transfers the trash to  the air. There are also health issues,   which I will discuss later. But the need  to just be rid of the waste got too real. Famously, there was an independent 2011  documentary called "Beijing Besieged by   Waste" (垃圾圍城) made by director Wang Jiuliang. Wang  got on a motorbike and traveled around Beijing,   mapping over 450 such illegal  landfills and dumps on Google Maps. It also called out the difficult lives of trash  pickers sifting through this toxic trash looking   for stuff to sell. And showed terrifying footage  of animals and livestock eating plastic bags. It was pretty horrid. The hard data  and undeniable footage sparked a   groundswell of public sentiment to which the  Mainland Chinese authorities had to respond. ## Waste Now an Asset The 12th 5-year Plan - which covers the  years between 2011 and 2015 - noted that   the country had urbanized very quickly but its  waste processing capacity could not keep up. Thus in April 2012, a new tariff  policy went into effect that made   waste-to-energy plants something  that people wanted to invest in. The policy deemed every ton of solid waste  to provide about 280 kilowatt-hours of power. The Chinese government pledged to  pay waste-to-energy plants about   0.65 RMB for each of those 280 kilowatt-hours. This subsidy is funded by the local grid company   with partial support from  a national power surcharge. Modern plants can generate more but everything  above that 280 kilowatt-hours per ton number   is paid at the local coal-fired  benchmark rate - which depending   on the locale is far lower at about  0.25 to 0.45 RMB per kilowatt-hour. So a plant owner-operator stands to earn about 182  RMB per ton just in subsidies - a number "locked   in" by policy. More if they generate extra  electricity but that’s basically negligible.   They can augment that power generation  money with additional revenue sources. The second biggest revenue source is the  waste disposal service fee paid by the   city. That is generally like 60 to 160 RMB per  ton but it gets put to bid so it can be lower. Beyond that, the plant can earn money  from selling heat to heat homes,   disposing of industrial sludge and waste,  selling power direct to AI data centers,   or selling leftover metal slag.  Not a lot but it’s honest work. So taking all that in, the average waste-to-energy  plant generates 250-350 RMB per ton of waste.   Cost with depreciation has been estimated by  industry groups to be about 200 RMB per ton,   leaving gross margins at about 25-75%.  Highly dependent on the plant itself. Companies also have a VAT refund  that they get for a few years. That   is a below-the-line benefit that  helps raise after-tax cash flow. Plants are largely made via the  Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT) model. The company signs a long-term concession with  the local government for a waste-to-energy plant. The company then raises the money - usually  by selling bonds - and builds the plant. Once done, the owner runs the plant  throughout the concession period,   (hopefully) earning a healthy  profit back on their capital. After the concession ends - usually about 20-30   years - the company transfers  the asset to the government. At 182RMB out of 250 to 350 total, the  government subsidy provides over half   of total revenue. Without it, the  business is not attractive - nigh   unsustainable considering how much  operating leverage is involved. But with the subsidies, we have a profitable  industry. Companies emerged to build and   run incinerators via the BOT model.  The largest being China Everbright,   Chongqing Sanfeng, Shanghai  Environment Protection Group,   and Zheneng Jinjiang Environment. There are  over 20 publicly listed companies in this space. ## Health Questions Now here, I need to mention  that incinerators receive   criticism for being linked to health side-effects. I have to note here that there are  so many unresolved questions. With   the answers to many them being: "We don't know." One major issue concerns particles  released in the air. Health-wise,   short and long-term exposure to  such particles can lead to chronic   conditions like bronchitis plus respiratory  and cardiovascular diseases like lung cancer. Environmentally, particles in the air contribute   to haze and smog. They also injure  plants and animals in the region. Particle counts can be reduced. Many years ago,   incinerator facilities added "afterburner  zones" to achieve the most complete possible   combustion. They have also implemented filters  to capture particles above a certain size. Even so, concerns remain about the impact of  these "nano-particles" remaining in the air.   Such particles can easily slip past the upper  airways of the nose and throat to directly   enter the lungs. But do they actually cause  health problems? This again we are not sure. Another issue of concern is the flue  gas. It depends on the waste composition,   but flue gas can contain hydrochloric  acid, sulfur dioxide, sulfur trioxide,   and nitric oxide. There are also  heavy metals like copper and the like. But what incinerators are most infamous for are  these super-toxins: Dioxins and furans. This   is a family of chlorinated hydrocarbons produced  when we burn items with chlorine, like plastics. We know of about 75 dioxins and 135  furans. They are resistant to light and   environmental breakdown so they accumulate  in livestock and foods - causing in people   reproductive problems, weak immune  systems, and potentially cancers. The only method to remove the dioxins and furans   is to not burn any chlorinated  plastics, which isn't practical. The modern philosophy is to use multiple  approaches including high heat - which is why   modern incinerators require that the waste spends  at least 2 seconds in temperatures of over 1,000   degrees Celsius - plus catalysts and filters to  reduce the dioxin level below a legislated amount. Is this okay? The evidence is controversial,  with claims of fraud. Monitoring equipment   is said to be unreliable. The fly ash is  still full of dioxins. Moreover, there   are still the other byproducts to consider like  mercury, sulfur dioxide, and hydrochloric acid. There are people who take the  position that an incinerator   cannot be redeemed in any circumstance. Period. ## NIMBY Concerns One of the major issues of building  these plants has been local sentiment,   something we might call NIMBYism. I mentioned earlier how Seoul banned  directly depositing waste into landfills,   particularly in the Gyeonggi and Incheon regions  outside Seoul proper. The curious thing about this   ban is that Seoul is short on incinerator  capacity because nobody wants them nearby. A 2022 plan to add a new incinerator in the area  of Mapo got tied up in court. In March 2026,   Seoul declined to appeal to the Supreme  Court and formally cancelled the project,   losing a thousand tons per day of capacity. Another proposed project in Gangnam -  where an incinerator already exists - is   called a "modernization" but Gangnam residents say   it is a shadow expansion. Right  now this one is at an impasse. These social concerns have many reasons.  There are the health and environmental   risks that we discussed earlier. But people  also feel concern about operational risks,   and the potentially massive  damage that accidents can cause. Such accident risk is not theoretical. In  December 2013, there was an explosion at   the Shanghai Jiangqiao Municipal Solid Waste  Incineration Plant, one of China's largest at   the time - caused by methane buildup inside  the plant. Three were reported to have died. ## The Hangzhou Plant The most notable NIMBY incident  occurred in the city of Hangzhou   in the Zhejiang Province,  the Hangzhou Jiufeng Plant. At the end of 2014, Hangzhou had a population  of 8.9 million and a 75% urbanization rate. Throughout 2014, those people  each day produced about 9,055   tons of municipal solid waste,  growing at a rate of 10% a year. To handle all that, Hangzhou had four existing   waste-to-energy plants capable  of handling 4,600 tons per day,   and one landfill (Hangzhou Tianziling)  designed for 1,920 to 4,000 tons per day. Unfortunately, one of the waste-to-energy  plants (Yuhang Jinjiang) had an aging design,   was too small with capacity of  just 400 tons per day, and faced   substantial local opposition. And the landfill  was scheduled to fill up in the next five years. So in April 2014, the local Hangzhou government  announced a new, larger plant in the Yuhang   district with capacity of 3,000 tons per day  - over a third of the city's trash production. It was - if I may say - a dumpster fire. Hangzhou  is a beautiful city with a long history. The   e-commerce giant Alibaba Group is headquartered  there along with DeepSeek and UniTree. Local residents also grow  Longjing tea in this area,   making the environmental impact doubly  important. This is their livelihood. My main point is that this is a rich  population that cares about where   they live and a waste-to-energy plant  some 20 miles southwest of the core   downtown area - even if it is somewhat  tucked away in a valley - makes people   nervous. 20,000 residents signed  a petition to protest the plant. The local government held a brief media  session promising to work with the people.   But when some geological equipment was  delivered to the site for a survey,   social media rumors exploded  and daily protests started. It came to a head in May 2014  when tens of thousands of people   clashed with police - causing extensive  property damage. Protestors blocked a   major highway in Yuhang and engaged  in hand-to-hand combat with police. State media reported that 39  people were hurt and no deaths,   which does not seem very believable to me.  When things calmed down, the local Hangzhou   government pledged that the plant be suspended  and go through a legal decision-making process. What went wrong here? A small group  inside the local government sited the   plant. They chose it on sensible, technocratic  grounds - tucked inside a former stone quarry   and accessible without going on residential  roads - but it was done without transparency. Then they announced it and tried  to rush it through without proper   public involvement. Since the public  wasn’t consulted, they got angry and   lashed out - forcing the government to  rally resources to defend its choice. This tragedy in three acts is called by academics  "Decide-Announce-Defend". It is also sometimes   jokingly called "Decide-Announce-Defend-Abandon",  for obvious reasons. ## Dealing with NIMBYism It is not possible to eliminate NIMBY  feelings. Even for the Communist Party. But what you can do is channel those feelings  earlier into the design and planning process,   where they are less likely to  interfere at a late stage. And   you can educate and engage with the  public to gain general acceptance. After the 2014 mass incident in Hangzhou, the  local government did not abandon the plant.   They concluded that the lack of transparency  in decision-making and the government’s   inconsistent statements diminished  the public trust so they rebooted it. The old operator was a state-owned startup  firm and their lack of experience was a   core source of distrust. They were replaced with  Everbright, a larger, more experienced company. The Hangzhou local government then  underwent a thorough Environmental   Impact Analysis with participation  from the public and an institute   from the central government. Documents in  the process were made available online. Local residents were brought into the  process. Government staff was mobilized   to visit and interview over 25,000 people,  collecting 500 suggestions and concerns.   A special disposal fee was attached to fund   these environmental initiatives. Local  residents were hired as supervisors. The Yuhang District also promised $360  million of financial support for tourism   and infrastructure. Whether this was  ever delivered, I am not too sure. The government and company also arranged local  hearings where Everbright experts answered   questions. In the second half of 2014, 5,000  local residents were bussed to other Everbright   facilities and shown how it worked - including  the presence of automatic monitoring equipment. A year later in April 2015, construction  restarted. The plant entered operations   in late November 2017. This largely created the   playbook for handling NIMBY sentiments.  A clear focus on community engagement,   careful site selection, automatic monitoring,  long standard EIA procedures, and more. It doesn't remove all the sentiments.  Blockades and NIMBY feelings continue to   exist - particularly in areas that already have a  few incinerators - but construction can move on. ## 400 In Progress So the 2012 tariff created an attractive  business model. The government learned   important lessons on community engagement  after 2014. Next comes the boom. The Chinese central government had  set a goal of about 591,000 daily   tons of capacity by 2020 and  worked backwards from there. In December 2017, the government ordered its  provincial governments to finish preparing   their site selections by 2018. Since a  plant takes about 15-24 months to build,   a 2018 site selection deadline gives  enough time to finish their plants by 2020. This created a concrete pipeline that you  can rush to hit the deadline. Between 2013   to 2017, China added just 41 new  waste-to-energy plants each year.   End of 2017, there was a total  of 360 across the nation. But in mid-2019, state media  reported that there were at   least 400 projects then in progress across  the nation. The boom was already underway. ## The New Era By 2020, China had 462 operational  waste-to-energy plants. National   incineration capacity reached 580,000 tons  per day - essentially hitting the target. But looking by region, progress was uneven:   East China hit their marks while West  and Central China did not. So the central   government raised the target to 800,000 tons  per day - with a focus on the rural areas. They also changed the subsidy structure.  Any plant started after January 2021 will   no longer get the 0.65 RMB per  kilowatt-hour subsidy. Moreover,   the subsidy will sunset after 82,500 hours for all  plants. The VAT refund was also partially lowered. The intention was to force the waste-to-energy  plants not to rely on power-generation - which   is not economical compared to solar and  wind - and turn to generating secondary   revenues like city waste disposal fees.  It also tried to make them more efficient. All projects were declared to be finished  by 2023. Thus by the end of 2024,   we have a total of 1,137 waste-to-energy  plants across the nation ... and what   has been commonly discussed in  media as a "regional imbalance". There is a lot of imbalance. 60% of  total incineration capacity is in five   provinces - Zhejiang, Jiangsu,  Guangdong, Shandong and Fujian. Between 2023 and 2025, the E20 Research  Institute reported that the average   capacity utilization rate of domestic  waste-to-energy incineration projects was   around 60%. Some plants have utilization  rates of 80+%. Others as low as 24%. About 16% of projects has a capacity  utilization rate below 50%. That is   rough for them because fixed costs are very  high. If these aren't being used, they are   losing money. A lot of money. Ergo why they  are going back and digging up older landfills. Growth will be slower post-2022. These  businesses must find new lines to replace   their subsidy revenue. In addition to just  charging the cities more - meaning citizens   pay more expensive trash collection fees -  there is also expanding into rural areas,   building plants abroad in places like Indonesia,  and developing new business lines like smelting. ## Conclusion As I said earlier, there are plenty of  voices that see this as an absolute win. In an FT article covering this,  a representative said at the end   "Having less waste is actually a good thing  ... It means the environment is improving". I do not know what to make of that. It's  nice to not have trash lying around for sure,   but sending it all into the air does  not sound very sustainable either. But there is one thing to consider. How the  Chinese government managed to expertly spur   private industrial development and build these  extremely unpopular items in a genuinely short   time, that is legitimately impressive.  There's something to be learned from it.

There were also economic issues. A waste-to-energy  plant has far higher capital costs at about
$66,000 to $120,000 per ton of daily capacity  - with some going as high as $365,000.
That high number is more of a developed  country estimate. These figures come out
of the World Bank's Decision Maker’s Guides  for Solid Waste Management Technologies, 2018.
A landfill by comparison costs about $5,000 to
$20,000 per daily ton of capacity  over its lifetime. So all in all,
it is 5-10 times cheaper to make a landfill.  Even less if that landfill is an illegal one.
## Besieged by Waste
A fierce debate raged early on - with  many saying that not addressing the
core issue of waste generation  is only treating the symptoms.
Without proper recycling, collection  or fees to incentivize reduction,
incineration just transfers the trash to  the air. There are also health issues,
which I will discuss later. But the need  to just be rid of the waste got too real.
Famously, there was an independent 2011  documentary called "Beijing Besieged by
Waste" (垃圾圍城) made by director Wang Jiuliang. Wang  got on a motorbike and traveled around Beijing,
mapping over 450 such illegal  landfills and dumps on Google Maps.
It also called out the difficult lives of trash  pickers sifting through this toxic trash looking
for stuff to sell. And showed terrifying footage  of animals and livestock eating plastic bags.
It was pretty horrid. The hard data  and undeniable footage sparked a
groundswell of public sentiment to which the  Mainland Chinese authorities had to respond.
## Waste Now an Asset
The 12th 5-year Plan - which covers the  years between 2011 and 2015 - noted that
the country had urbanized very quickly but its  waste processing capacity could not keep up.
Thus in April 2012, a new tariff  policy went into effect that made
waste-to-energy plants something  that people wanted to invest in.
The policy deemed every ton of solid waste  to provide about 280 kilowatt-hours of power.
The Chinese government pledged to  pay waste-to-energy plants about
0.65 RMB for each of those 280 kilowatt-hours.
This subsidy is funded by the local grid company
with partial support from  a national power surcharge.
Modern plants can generate more but everything  above that 280 kilowatt-hours per ton number
is paid at the local coal-fired  benchmark rate - which depending
on the locale is far lower at about  0.25 to 0.45 RMB per kilowatt-hour.
So a plant owner-operator stands to earn about 182  RMB per ton just in subsidies - a number "locked
in" by policy. More if they generate extra  electricity but that’s basically negligible.
They can augment that power generation  money with additional revenue sources.
The second biggest revenue source is the  waste disposal service fee paid by the
city. That is generally like 60 to 160 RMB per  ton but it gets put to bid so it can be lower.
Beyond that, the plant can earn money  from selling heat to heat homes,
disposing of industrial sludge and waste,  selling power direct to AI data centers,
or selling leftover metal slag.  Not a lot but it’s honest work.
So taking all that in, the average waste-to-energy  plant generates 250-350 RMB per ton of waste.
Cost with depreciation has been estimated by  industry groups to be about 200 RMB per ton,
leaving gross margins at about 25-75%.  Highly dependent on the plant itself.
Companies also have a VAT refund  that they get for a few years. That
is a below-the-line benefit that  helps raise after-tax cash flow.
Plants are largely made via the  Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT) model.
The company signs a long-term concession with  the local government for a waste-to-energy plant.
The company then raises the money - usually  by selling bonds - and builds the plant.
Once done, the owner runs the plant  throughout the concession period,
(hopefully) earning a healthy  profit back on their capital.
After the concession ends - usually about 20-30
years - the company transfers  the asset to the government.
At 182RMB out of 250 to 350 total, the  government subsidy provides over half
of total revenue. Without it, the  business is not attractive - nigh
unsustainable considering how much  operating leverage is involved.
But with the subsidies, we have a profitable  industry. Companies emerged to build and
run incinerators via the BOT model.  The largest being China Everbright,
Chongqing Sanfeng, Shanghai  Environment Protection Group,
and Zheneng Jinjiang Environment. There are  over 20 publicly listed companies in this space.
## Health Questions
Now here, I need to mention  that incinerators receive
criticism for being linked to health side-effects.
I have to note here that there are  so many unresolved questions. With
the answers to many them being: "We don't know."
One major issue concerns particles  released in the air. Health-wise,
short and long-term exposure to  such particles can lead to chronic
conditions like bronchitis plus respiratory  and cardiovascular diseases like lung cancer.
Environmentally, particles in the air contribute
to haze and smog. They also injure  plants and animals in the region.
Particle counts can be reduced. Many years ago,
incinerator facilities added "afterburner  zones" to achieve the most complete possible
combustion. They have also implemented filters  to capture particles above a certain size.
Even so, concerns remain about the impact of  these "nano-particles" remaining in the air.
Such particles can easily slip past the upper  airways of the nose and throat to directly
enter the lungs. But do they actually cause  health problems? This again we are not sure.
Another issue of concern is the flue  gas. It depends on the waste composition,
but flue gas can contain hydrochloric  acid, sulfur dioxide, sulfur trioxide,
and nitric oxide. There are also  heavy metals like copper and the like.
But what incinerators are most infamous for are  these super-toxins: Dioxins and furans. This
is a family of chlorinated hydrocarbons produced  when we burn items with chlorine, like plastics.
We know of about 75 dioxins and 135  furans. They are resistant to light and
environmental breakdown so they accumulate  in livestock and foods - causing in people
reproductive problems, weak immune  systems, and potentially cancers.
The only method to remove the dioxins and furans
is to not burn any chlorinated  plastics, which isn't practical.
The modern philosophy is to use multiple  approaches including high heat - which is why
modern incinerators require that the waste spends  at least 2 seconds in temperatures of over 1,000
degrees Celsius - plus catalysts and filters to  reduce the dioxin level below a legislated amount.
Is this okay? The evidence is controversial,  with claims of fraud. Monitoring equipment
is said to be unreliable. The fly ash is  still full of dioxins. Moreover, there
are still the other byproducts to consider like  mercury, sulfur dioxide, and hydrochloric acid.
There are people who take the  position that an incinerator
cannot be redeemed in any circumstance. Period.
## NIMBY Concerns
One of the major issues of building  these plants has been local sentiment,
something we might call NIMBYism.
I mentioned earlier how Seoul banned  directly depositing waste into landfills,
particularly in the Gyeonggi and Incheon regions  outside Seoul proper. The curious thing about this
ban is that Seoul is short on incinerator  capacity because nobody wants them nearby.
A 2022 plan to add a new incinerator in the area  of Mapo got tied up in court. In March 2026,
Seoul declined to appeal to the Supreme  Court and formally cancelled the project,
losing a thousand tons per day of capacity.
Another proposed project in Gangnam -  where an incinerator already exists - is
called a "modernization" but Gangnam residents say
it is a shadow expansion. Right  now this one is at an impasse.
These social concerns have many reasons.  There are the health and environmental
risks that we discussed earlier. But people  also feel concern about operational risks,
and the potentially massive  damage that accidents can cause.
Such accident risk is not theoretical. In  December 2013, there was an explosion at
the Shanghai Jiangqiao Municipal Solid Waste  Incineration Plant, one of China's largest at
the time - caused by methane buildup inside  the plant. Three were reported to have died.
## The Hangzhou Plant
The most notable NIMBY incident  occurred in the city of Hangzhou
in the Zhejiang Province,  the Hangzhou Jiufeng Plant.
At the end of 2014, Hangzhou had a population  of 8.9 million and a 75% urbanization rate.
Throughout 2014, those people  each day produced about 9,055
tons of municipal solid waste,  growing at a rate of 10% a year.
To handle all that, Hangzhou had four existing
waste-to-energy plants capable  of handling 4,600 tons per day,
and one landfill (Hangzhou Tianziling)  designed for 1,920 to 4,000 tons per day.
Unfortunately, one of the waste-to-energy  plants (Yuhang Jinjiang) had an aging design,
was too small with capacity of  just 400 tons per day, and faced
substantial local opposition. And the landfill  was scheduled to fill up in the next five years.
So in April 2014, the local Hangzhou government  announced a new, larger plant in the Yuhang
district with capacity of 3,000 tons per day  - over a third of the city's trash production.
It was - if I may say - a dumpster fire. Hangzhou  is a beautiful city with a long history. The
e-commerce giant Alibaba Group is headquartered  there along with DeepSeek and UniTree.
Local residents also grow  Longjing tea in this area,
making the environmental impact doubly  important. This is their livelihood.
My main point is that this is a rich  population that cares about where
they live and a waste-to-energy plant  some 20 miles southwest of the core
downtown area - even if it is somewhat  tucked away in a valley - makes people
nervous. 20,000 residents signed  a petition to protest the plant.
The local government held a brief media  session promising to work with the people.
But when some geological equipment was  delivered to the site for a survey,
social media rumors exploded  and daily protests started.
It came to a head in May 2014  when tens of thousands of people
clashed with police - causing extensive  property damage. Protestors blocked a
major highway in Yuhang and engaged  in hand-to-hand combat with police.
State media reported that 39  people were hurt and no deaths,
which does not seem very believable to me.  When things calmed down, the local Hangzhou
government pledged that the plant be suspended  and go through a legal decision-making process.
What went wrong here? A small group  inside the local government sited the
plant. They chose it on sensible, technocratic  grounds - tucked inside a former stone quarry
and accessible without going on residential  roads - but it was done without transparency.
Then they announced it and tried  to rush it through without proper
public involvement. Since the public  wasn’t consulted, they got angry and
lashed out - forcing the government to  rally resources to defend its choice.
This tragedy in three acts is called by academics  "Decide-Announce-Defend". It is also sometimes
jokingly called "Decide-Announce-Defend-Abandon",  for obvious reasons.
## Dealing with NIMBYism
It is not possible to eliminate NIMBY  feelings. Even for the Communist Party.
But what you can do is channel those feelings  earlier into the design and planning process,
where they are less likely to  interfere at a late stage. And
you can educate and engage with the  public to gain general acceptance.
After the 2014 mass incident in Hangzhou, the  local government did not abandon the plant.
They concluded that the lack of transparency  in decision-making and the government’s
inconsistent statements diminished  the public trust so they rebooted it.
The old operator was a state-owned startup  firm and their lack of experience was a
core source of distrust. They were replaced with  Everbright, a larger, more experienced company.
The Hangzhou local government then  underwent a thorough Environmental
Impact Analysis with participation  from the public and an institute
from the central government. Documents in  the process were made available online.
Local residents were brought into the  process. Government staff was mobilized
to visit and interview over 25,000 people,  collecting 500 suggestions and concerns.
A special disposal fee was attached to fund
these environmental initiatives. Local  residents were hired as supervisors.
The Yuhang District also promised $360  million of financial support for tourism
and infrastructure. Whether this was  ever delivered, I am not too sure.
The government and company also arranged local  hearings where Everbright experts answered
questions. In the second half of 2014, 5,000  local residents were bussed to other Everbright
facilities and shown how it worked - including  the presence of automatic monitoring equipment.
A year later in April 2015, construction  restarted. The plant entered operations
in late November 2017. This largely created the
playbook for handling NIMBY sentiments.  A clear focus on community engagement,
careful site selection, automatic monitoring,  long standard EIA procedures, and more.
It doesn't remove all the sentiments.  Blockades and NIMBY feelings continue to
exist - particularly in areas that already have a  few incinerators - but construction can move on.
## 400 In Progress
So the 2012 tariff created an attractive  business model. The government learned
important lessons on community engagement  after 2014. Next comes the boom.
The Chinese central government had  set a goal of about 591,000 daily
tons of capacity by 2020 and  worked backwards from there.
In December 2017, the government ordered its  provincial governments to finish preparing
their site selections by 2018. Since a  plant takes about 15-24 months to build,
a 2018 site selection deadline gives  enough time to finish their plants by 2020.
This created a concrete pipeline that you  can rush to hit the deadline. Between 2013
to 2017, China added just 41 new  waste-to-energy plants each year.
End of 2017, there was a total  of 360 across the nation.
But in mid-2019, state media  reported that there were at
least 400 projects then in progress across  the nation. The boom was already underway.
## The New Era
By 2020, China had 462 operational  waste-to-energy plants. National
incineration capacity reached 580,000 tons  per day - essentially hitting the target.
But looking by region, progress was uneven:
East China hit their marks while West  and Central China did not. So the central
government raised the target to 800,000 tons  per day - with a focus on the rural areas.
They also changed the subsidy structure.  Any plant started after January 2021 will
no longer get the 0.65 RMB per  kilowatt-hour subsidy. Moreover,
the subsidy will sunset after 82,500 hours for all  plants. The VAT refund was also partially lowered.
The intention was to force the waste-to-energy  plants not to rely on power-generation - which
is not economical compared to solar and  wind - and turn to generating secondary
revenues like city waste disposal fees.  It also tried to make them more efficient.
All projects were declared to be finished  by 2023. Thus by the end of 2024,
we have a total of 1,137 waste-to-energy  plants across the nation ... and what
has been commonly discussed in  media as a "regional imbalance".
There is a lot of imbalance. 60% of  total incineration capacity is in five
provinces - Zhejiang, Jiangsu,  Guangdong, Shandong and Fujian.
Between 2023 and 2025, the E20 Research  Institute reported that the average
capacity utilization rate of domestic  waste-to-energy incineration projects was
around 60%. Some plants have utilization  rates of 80+%. Others as low as 24%.
About 16% of projects has a capacity  utilization rate below 50%. That is
rough for them because fixed costs are very  high. If these aren't being used, they are
losing money. A lot of money. Ergo why they  are going back and digging up older landfills.
Growth will be slower post-2022. These  businesses must find new lines to replace
their subsidy revenue. In addition to just  charging the cities more - meaning citizens
pay more expensive trash collection fees -  there is also expanding into rural areas,
building plants abroad in places like Indonesia,  and developing new business lines like smelting.
## Conclusion
As I said earlier, there are plenty of  voices that see this as an absolute win.
In an FT article covering this,  a representative said at the end
"Having less waste is actually a good thing  ... It means the environment is improving".
I do not know what to make of that. It's  nice to not have trash lying around for sure,
but sending it all into the air does  not sound very sustainable either.
But there is one thing to consider. How the  Chinese government managed to expertly spur
private industrial development and build these  extremely unpopular items in a genuinely short
time, that is legitimately impressive.  There's something to be learned from it.
